 Best Budget Portable Power Station (2026): Real LiFePO4 Picks Under $300
 By Editorial Team · Updated September 14, 2026
 Affiliate disclosure: We independently research and test every product. When you buy through links on this page, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 Quick answer
 The Bluetti EB3A is the best budget portable power station overall in 2026 — a real 268Wh LiFePO4
battery, 600W continuous output, and a street price around $179 , the cheapest true-LiFePO4 entry
worth buying. Budget power stations only stay a good deal if the battery inside is actually LiFePO4 :
those cells rate for 3,000-6,000+ cycles , while the NMC lithium-ion cells still common in cheap
no-name Amazon units typically last just 500-1,000 cycles , according to battery-industry lifecycle
testing. All five picks below are named-brand LiFePO4 units between $179 and $299 — not the unlabeled
generic imports that make “budget” a trap instead of a deal.
 Every unit here uses the same LiFePO4 chemistry the site’s higher-end picks do — the difference at this
price point is capacity, recharge speed, and cycle life, not battery safety. A $500 LiFePO4 station
rated for 2,500 cycles works out to well under a dollar per use over its lifetime; a cheaper NMC unit
hitting end-of-life at 500-1,000 cycles often costs more per use despite the lower sticker price, per
the same lifecycle data. Below are the five budget-tier picks worth that math.
 Budget power stations at a glance
 Model Best for Capacity Continuous / Surge Recharge Price Rating 
 Bluetti EB3A Best overall budget 268Wh 600W / 1,200W ~1hr (wall) ~$179 ★★★★★ 
 Anker SOLIX C300 Best value 288Wh 300W / 600W ~1hr (wall) ~$199 ★★★★½ 
 EcoFlow River 3 Fastest recharge 245Wh 300W / 600W ~60 min (wall) ~$199-229 ★★★★½ 
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus Longest cycle life 288Wh 300W / — ~2hrs (wall) ~$249 ★★★★★ 
 EcoFlow River 3 Plus Best if you might expand 286Wh 600W / 1,200W ~1hr (wall) ~$269-299 ★★★★☆ 
 1. Bluetti EB3A — Best Overall Budget Pick
 Bluetti EB3A (268Wh)
 Best overall budget · ~$179 · 268Wh LiFePO4 · 600W AC
 268Wh of real LiFePO4 capacity and a 600W continuous output (1,200W surge) for budget-power-bank money — enough for phones, a CPAP, or a mini fridge for a few hours.
 Recharges from a wall outlet in about an hour, faster than most units at this price.
 At ~10.1 lb it's easy to keep in a car or closet without dedicating real storage space to it.
 The EB3A is the cheapest unit on this list that still checks every box a budget buyer actually needs:
real LiFePO4, a fast recharge, and enough output for small electronics. Only need to charge phones and
small gear? Bluetti’s own AC2A goes even cheaper at 204.8Wh/300W. See our
 best power station for camping guide for how it
compares on the trail specifically.
 2. Anker SOLIX C300 — Best Value
 Anker SOLIX C300 (288Wh)
 Best value · ~$199 · 288Wh LiFePO4 · 300W AC (600W surge)
 288Wh — the most capacity per dollar of any pick here — with a 300W continuous output and 600W surge for light appliances.
 Anker's standard 5-year warranty applies automatically, no product registration step required.
 Wall recharge in about an hour keeps it ready between weekend trips or outages.
 If the goal is the most watt-hours for the least money without dropping to an unproven no-name brand,
the C300 wins that math. See our full Anker SOLIX C300 review 
for why the “C300” name now covers three genuinely different variants, or our Anker SOLIX vs.
Bluetti comparison for how the brand’s larger units stack up if
you outgrow it.
 3. EcoFlow River 3 — Fastest Recharge
 EcoFlow River 3 (245Wh)
 Fastest recharge · ~$199-229 · 245Wh LiFePO4 · 300W AC (600W X-Boost)
 245Wh LiFePO4 in a 7.8 lb body — one of the lightest true-LiFePO4 stations available at this price.
 0-100% wall recharge in about 60 minutes, per EcoFlow's own published specs, among the fastest at any price.
 X-Boost mode pushes continuous output to 600W for light appliances that would otherwise trip a 300W ceiling.
 For buyers who mainly need it charged and ready — not sitting on a trickle charger for hours — the
River 3’s recharge speed is the deciding spec. Read our
 full EcoFlow River 3 review for the complete breakdown. Don’t
confuse it with the similarly-specced but older EcoFlow River 2 —
despite the lower model number sounding newer, it’s the prior generation and currently lists for more.
 4. Jackery Explorer 300 Plus — Longest Cycle Life
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus (288Wh)
 Longest cycle life · ~$249 · 288Wh LiFePO4 · 300W AC
 Jackery's own materials cite the longest published cycle-life range of any pick here — 3,000-4,000 cycles to 80% capacity — though the exact figure isn't consistent across Jackery's sources. The newer [Explorer 300 v2](/reviews/jackery-explorer-300-v2-review/) it's been replaced by rates more consistently at 4,000+.
 288Wh capacity and a 300W continuous output cover a CPAP for 3-5 nights on a charge without a top-up.
 At ~8.3 lb it's built around portability first, the pick to grab for a weekend away rather than a fixed spot at home.
 If this is going to be a daily-use unit for years rather than an occasional backup, the 300 Plus’s
cycle-life edge pays for itself over time — though it’s worth knowing Jackery has replaced it with the
 Explorer 300 v2 direct from their own site; our full
Jackery Explorer 300 Plus review covers the generation
change in detail. See our
 best power station for camping picks for how it
performs outdoors specifically.
 5. EcoFlow River 3 Plus — Best If You Might Need to Expand
 EcoFlow River 3 Plus (286Wh)
 Best if you might expand · ~$269-299 · 286Wh LiFePO4 · 600W AC (1,200W surge)
 The only pick on this list with a battery expansion path — add an EB300 or EB600 pack later instead of replacing the whole unit.
 600W continuous output (1,200W surge) is double the base River 3's ceiling, covering more appliances at once.
 Sub-10ms UPS switchover keeps sensitive electronics running through a power blip without a reboot.
 It’s the priciest pick here, but the only one that scales up instead of becoming e-waste if your needs
outgrow it. Read our
 full EcoFlow River 3 Plus review for the complete breakdown.
 What actually matters when buying budget
 Check for the words “LiFePO4” or “LFP” in the listing. If a cheap unit only says “lithium battery”
with no chemistry named and advertises fewer than 1,000 charge cycles, assume it’s NMC and will need
replacing in 2-3 years of regular use, not 8-12. Our Duracell power station
review covers a real current example of a trusted brand name
built on that older chemistry, not LiFePO4.
 Cost-per-cycle beats sticker price. A $500 LiFePO4 unit rated for 2,500 cycles costs well under
$1 per use over its life; a $150 NMC unit hitting end-of-life at 500-800 cycles can cost more per use
despite the lower price tag. See our
 how long a power station really lasts guide for the
full cycle-life math.
 Match capacity to what you’ll actually run. Every pick here tops out around 300-600W continuous —
fine for phones, lights, a CPAP, or a mini fridge, not a power tool or full-size refrigerator. Our
 power station sizing guide walks through the wattage
math if you’re unsure.
 Recharge speed matters more than it looks on a spec sheet if you’re using the unit daily rather
than occasionally — an hour-long wall recharge means it’s ready again well before bedtime.
 A 5-year warranty on a $200 unit is a good sign , not overkill — it’s the manufacturer backing the
same LiFePO4 durability claim the price is supposed to reflect. Buying refurbished 
can push the price even lower, but check the warranty term first — it can drop as low as 6 months
depending on the seller.
 Need more capacity than any of these five offer? Our
 best portable power station picks cover the full lineup, from
this budget tier up to whole-home backup units.
 The bottom line
 The Bluetti EB3A is the best budget portable power station for most buyers in 2026 — real LiFePO4,
fast recharge, and the lowest price on this list that doesn’t cut the one corner that actually matters.
The Anker SOLIX C300 gets the most watt-hours per dollar, the EcoFlow River 3 recharges
fastest, the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus is rated for the most charge cycles (albeit across a
disputed 3,000-4,000 range), and the EcoFlow River 3 Plus is the only one that can grow with an
expansion battery later. Whichever you pick, the one non-negotiable at this price point is the
battery chemistry — LiFePO4 or don’t buy it. See our direct Bluetti EB3A vs EcoFlow River 3 Plus vs
Anker SOLIX C300 three-way comparison for how the top
three of these five stack up on warranty length and cycle life, not just price.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Are budget power stations actually safe, or do you get what you pay for? It depends entirely on the battery chemistry, not the price tag. LiFePO4 (LFP) cells rate for 3,000-6,000+ cycles and handle heat safely, while NMC lithium-ion cells common in cheap no-name Amazon units typically last only 500-1,000 cycles, per battery-industry lifecycle testing. All five picks below use real LiFePO4 — if a listing doesn't state the chemistry and advertises a cycle rating under 1,000, assume it's NMC.
 What's the real difference between these five budget picks? Capacity, recharge speed, and cycle life, mostly. The Bluetti EB3A (268Wh, ~$179) and Anker SOLIX C300 (288Wh, ~$199) are the cheapest true-LiFePO4 entries; the EcoFlow River 3 (245Wh, ~$199-229) recharges fastest at about 60 minutes; the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus (288Wh, ~$249) is rated for the most charge cycles among these five, though Jackery's own materials cite a disputed 3,000-4,000 range rather than a single figure; and the EcoFlow River 3 Plus (286Wh, ~$269-299) is the only one with an expansion battery option if your needs grow.
 Should I just buy the cheapest power station I can find instead? Only if it's still LiFePO4 — otherwise it's a false economy. A $500 LiFePO4 unit rated for 2,500+ cycles works out to well under a dollar per cycle over its life, while a cheaper NMC unit hitting end-of-life at 500-1,000 cycles costs more per use despite the lower sticker price. At the budget tier specifically, sticking to a named brand with a published LiFePO4 spec is what keeps the math in your favor.

Bluetti’s fast-charge mode can take it from 0-80% in about 30 minutes, though standard AC charging runs 1.3-1.8 hours. It carries a 2-year warranty, shorter than the others on this list.
 Best for: short trips or emergencies where fast charging and surge headroom matter more than total runtime.

 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus — Most Established Brand Under $300

It’s the lightest full-size unit here at 8.27 lbs, and Jackery’s 3+2-year warranty structure (5 years total when registered) is the longest of the four.
 Best for: device charging, small electronics, and buyers who prioritize warranty length and brand track record over raw output.

 The C300 matches the Jackery’s 288Wh capacity and adds a 600W surge rating, a faster 50-minute charge time, and a longer 5-year warranty — typically at the lowest price of any station in this comparison. Anker rates it at just 25dB of operating noise from 3.3 feet away, and it includes 140W two-way USB-C fast charging for topping off laptops or the station itself from a power bank.
 Best for: the tightest budget, or as a second/backup unit alongside a larger station.

Best Portable Power Stations Under $500 in 2026 | VoltVanguard Best Portable Power Stations Under $500 in 2026
 Updated September 2026
 Affiliate disclosure: This site contains affiliate links. We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you if you buy through them. We never accept payment for coverage and our picks are editorial. Quick answer: The best portable power station under $500 is the Anker SOLIX C800 Plus ($499) — a 768Wh LiFePO4 battery with a 1,200W inverter and a sub-hour recharge, enough for CPAP backup, a mini-fridge, or a weekend of camping. If you want something smaller and lighter, the Anker SOLIX C300 ($219) is the best runner-up: an 8.2 lb, 288Wh unit built for backpacks and day trips rather than home backup.
 A sub-$500 budget rules out the big 2,000Wh-class units that can run a full refrigerator through a multi-day outage, but it still covers a wide range of real needs: charging phones and laptops, running a CPAP machine overnight, keeping a router and a few lights on, or powering a job site tool for an afternoon. This guide compares the four power stations worth considering under $500, breaks down which price tier fits which use case, and explains exactly what you are trading away as you move down in budget.
 Best Portable Power Stations Under $500, Compared
 Power Station Capacity Continuous / Surge AC Recharge Price Best For 
 Anker SOLIX C800 Plus 768Wh LiFePO4 1,200W / 2,400W ~46-48 min $499 Best overall under $500 
 Anker SOLIX C300 288Wh LiFePO4 300W / 600W ~58 min $219 Most portable, best budget pick 
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus 288Wh LiFePO4 300W / 600W ~1.5 hours $249 Best build quality and brand support 
 EGO POWER+ PST1400 Uses EGO 56V ARC batteries (sold separately) 1,400W / 2,800W Depends on charger used $349 (batteries extra) Homeowners already in the EGO ecosystem 
 Anker SOLIX C800 Plus: Best Overall Under $500
 The Anker SOLIX C800 Plus is the sweet spot of this price bracket: it packs 768Wh into a 1,200W-continuous (2,400W surge) inverter, which is enough headroom for a CPAP machine with a humidifier, a mini-fridge, a laptop, and a phone charger running at the same time. At $499 it works out to about $0.65 per watt-hour, undercutting the larger Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 on price while actually recharging faster.
 Who it is for: buyers who want the most home-backup capability they can get without crossing $500 — CPAP users, apartment dwellers who need mini-fridge backup, and weekend campers who want more than a phone-charging brick.
 Standout strengths: a 46-48 minute AC recharge at 1,000W (among the fastest in this capacity class), a 300W solar input for faster off-grid charging, and LiFePO4 cell chemistry rated for 3,000+ cycles.
 Honest trade-offs: at 22.3 lbs it is not backpack-portable, and 1,200W continuous output will not run a space heater, a full-size refrigerator, or a portable air conditioner for long. Read the full Anker SOLIX C800 Plus review for complete testing notes, or check the Anker SOLIX C800 Plus price on Amazon .
 Anker SOLIX C300: Best Budget and Most Portable Pick
 The Anker SOLIX C300 trades capacity for portability. Its 288Wh LiFePO4 battery will not run a refrigerator, but at 8.2 lbs it fits in a daypack, and its 58-minute AC recharge and 140W USB-C PD port make it the fastest-charging unit in its size class. At $219 it is also the least expensive station on this list.
 Who it is for: day hikers, backpackers, commuters who want a laptop-charging backup, and anyone building a compact emergency kit who does not need whole-room backup power.
 Standout strengths: lightest unit here by a wide margin, fastest USB-C PD output (140W) in this roundup, and a recharge time that beats units twice its capacity.
 Honest trade-offs: 300W continuous output rules out anything with a motor or heating element, and 288Wh covers a single overnight CPAP run at best. Solar input tops out at 100W, so full solar recharges take 3-4 hours in good sun. See the Anker SOLIX C300 review for full specs, or check the Anker SOLIX C300 price on Amazon .
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus: Best Build Quality and Brand Support
 The Jackery Explorer 300 Plus matches the Anker SOLIX C300's 288Wh capacity almost spec-for-spec, but costs about $30 more. What that premium buys is Jackery's longer track record, broader accessory ecosystem, and a support network that many first-time buyers find reassuring.
 Who it is for: campers and preppers who specifically want Jackery's build quality and are willing to pay a small premium over the cheapest option, or buyers who already own Jackery solar panels or accessories.
 Standout strengths: rugged housing, straightforward controls, and a large base of user reviews and troubleshooting resources.
 Honest trade-offs: AC recharge takes about 1.5 hours versus the C300's 58 minutes, and its 100W USB-C PD port is noticeably slower than the C300's 140W. For a full category-by-category breakdown, see our Anker SOLIX C300 vs Jackery Explorer 300 Plus comparison , or check the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus price on Amazon .
 EGO POWER+ PST1400: Best Only If You Already Own EGO Batteries
 The EGO POWER+ PST1400 has the highest continuous output on this list at 1,400W (2,800W surge), and its $349 sticker price looks like the best deal here — until you notice it ships with no batteries. EGO's power station is designed to run on the same 56V ARC Lithium batteries used in EGO lawn tools, which are sold separately.
 Who it is for: homeowners who already own two or more EGO 56V batteries for a mower, trimmer, or chainsaw and want those batteries to double as emergency backup power.
 Standout strengths: highest continuous wattage in this roundup, and genuine dual-purpose value for existing EGO tool owners since the batteries are not a sunk cost.
 Honest trade-offs: buying batteries from scratch to match the Anker SOLIX C1000's capacity brings the EGO's real-world cost to well over $1,000, which erases its price advantage for anyone starting from zero. Our full Anker SOLIX C1000 vs EGO PST1400 comparison breaks down the true cost math, or check the EGO POWER+ PST1400 price on Amazon .
 How to Choose a Power Station Under $500
 What Can a Sub-$500 Power Station Actually Run?
 In this price range, expect to comfortably run phones, laptops, routers, LED lighting, small fans, and most CPAP machines. The 768Wh Anker SOLIX C800 Plus stretches to a mini-fridge or a single space-heater cycle on its 1,200W inverter. None of the units here are built to run a central air conditioner, an electric range, or a full-size refrigerator for an extended outage — for that, look at 2,000Wh-class stations, which start well above $500. Use our power station wattage calculator to match your specific appliances against these specs before buying.
 Price Tiers: What Changes as You Spend More
 Sub-$500 power stations roughly break into three tiers, and understanding them prevents both overspending and buying something that cannot do the job.
 Under $250 (Anker SOLIX C300, Jackery Explorer 300 Plus): 288Wh-class units built for single-device backup — phones, laptops, a CPAP for one night, or a camp light setup. Continuous output tops out around 300W, so anything with a motor or heating element is off the table.
 $250-$350 (EGO POWER+ PST1400 and similar): this tier is where "sticker price" and "real price" start to diverge. A bare power-station shell with no batteries can look like a bargain until you price out the batteries that make it usable. Read the fine print on what is actually included before comparing prices across this tier.
 $350-$500 (Anker SOLIX C800 Plus): the most capable tier available before crossing into 1,000Wh-class territory above $500. Expect 700-800Wh of capacity, 1,000-1,200W continuous output, and recharge times under an hour — enough for genuine light home backup, not just device charging.
 LiFePO4 vs Older Lithium-Ion Chemistry
 Every station on this list uses LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) cells, and that is not a coincidence — it is now the standard chemistry at every price point because it lasts 3,000+ charge cycles compared with 500-800 for older lithium-ion cells, and it is significantly more resistant to thermal runaway. If a sub-$500 power station you are considering does not specify LiFePO4 or LFP in its listing, treat that as a red flag and check the fine print before buying. The cycle-life difference matters most if you plan to use the station regularly rather than as a once-a-year emergency backup: a LiFePO4 unit cycled daily for years will still hold a meaningful charge long after an older lithium-ion pack has degraded past usefulness.
 How Much Capacity Do You Actually Need?
 Work backward from your worst-case use, not your average use. A single overnight CPAP run needs roughly 60-100Wh; a mini-fridge cycling on and off needs 400-600Wh over 24 hours; a work laptop plus phone charging for a full day needs under 150Wh. If your primary goal is short power outages or weekend trips, 288Wh (the Anker SOLIX C300 or Jackery Explorer 300 Plus) is often enough. If you want a buffer for a fridge, CPAP, and lighting together, the 768Wh Anker SOLIX C800 Plus is the better fit. For a broader look at sizing logic across all budgets, see how to choose a portable power station , and if your needs turn out to be larger than 800Wh, our best 1000W portable power stations roundup covers the next tier up.
 Solar Charging on a Budget
 All four stations here accept solar input, but the ceiling varies a lot. The Anker SOLIX C300 caps out at 100W of solar input, meaning a full recharge in good sun takes 3-4 hours. The Anker SOLIX C800 Plus accepts up to 300W, cutting that recharge window roughly in half. If off-grid solar charging is a priority — for extended camping trips or true off-grid backup — that gap alone can be worth paying the extra $280 to move up from the C300 to the C800 Plus, even if you do not need the extra battery capacity for your daily loads.
 Common Mistakes When Buying a Budget Power Station
 The most common mistake is comparing sticker prices without checking what is included — the EGO PST1400 is the clearest example, since its $349 price excludes the batteries that make it function. The second most common mistake is ignoring AC recharge time: a station that takes 1.5-2 hours to refill is far less useful during a multi-outage week than one that recharges in under an hour. A third mistake is confusing continuous and surge wattage: a 300W station with a 600W surge rating will still trip and shut off if you plug in a device with a 700W startup draw, even briefly, so always size against continuous wattage for anything you plan to run for more than a few seconds. Finally, buyers sometimes skip checking warranty length — all four stations here carry multi-year warranties, but coverage terms and what counts as normal wear vary by brand, so it is worth reading the fine print before you need to file a claim.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best portable power station under $500? The Anker SOLIX C800 Plus is the best all-around pick at $499, offering 768Wh of capacity and a 1,200W inverter. For a lighter, more portable option, the Anker SOLIX C300 at $219 is the better fit.
 Can a power station under $500 run a refrigerator? The 768Wh Anker SOLIX C800 Plus can run a modern mini-fridge or briefly cycle a full-size refrigerator, but none of the stations in this price range are sized for running a full-size fridge through a multi-day outage. For that, look at 2,000Wh-class stations above $500.
 Is a cheaper power station with standard lithium-ion cells worth buying instead? Generally no. LiFePO4 cells, used in every station in this guide, last 3,000+ cycles versus 500-800 for older lithium-ion chemistry and are far safer against thermal runaway, which is why LiFePO4 has become the standard even at budget price points.
 Is the EGO POWER+ PST1400 actually a budget option? Only if you already own EGO 56V batteries. Its $349 price excludes batteries entirely, and buying enough of them from scratch to match a comparable Anker or Jackery station can push the real cost above $1,000.
 How long does a sub-$500 power station take to recharge? It varies widely: the Anker SOLIX C800 Plus and Anker SOLIX C300 both recharge via AC in under an hour, while the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus takes about 1.5 hours. Faster AC recharge matters most if you expect repeated short outages rather than one long one.

Jackery’s spec table doesn’t print a solar-input max; its FAQ points to SolarSaga panels up to 100 W. We couldn’t find a verified Amazon.com listing for this exact model, so we link to Jackery only.
 Jackery product page 
 How to choose (with easy runtime math)
 1. Add up your “must-run” watts
 Look at the label or charger brick on each thing you want running at the same time. Add them up. That total has to stay under the station’s rated watts. Not the surge. Not the boost.
 2. Guess how long, then do this math
 Hours ≈ Wh ÷ device watts × 0.85 
 The 0.85 covers the energy the station loses turning battery power into wall power. It’s a rough rule, not a promise. Real runtime depends on the device, temperature, and battery age.
 Example load (steady) 
 ~288 Wh station 
 ~1,024 Wh station 
 15 W (say, a modem + router) 
 about 16 hours 
 about 58 hours 
 60 W (say, a CPAP without heated humidifier — check yours) 
 about 4 hours 
 about 14.5 hours 
 100 W (a few lights + a fan + phone charging) 
 about 2.4 hours 
 about 8.7 hours 
 These are our own arithmetic examples using the formula above, not test results. The watts are examples; use your device’s real number. 
 Rather skip the math? Try our portable power station size calculator : add your devices, and it shows the battery size you need.
 3. Fridge? Size up.
 A fridge compressor cycles on and off, and it kicks hard when it starts. The ~300 Wh boxes aren’t fridge batteries. The ~1 kWh boxes can help for a while. For the full walkthrough, read How Long Will a Solar Generator Run a Fridge? and How Much Solar Generator Do I Need? 
 4. Plan the recharge
 Wall first, before the storm. Solar is day two, if the sky cooperates. Panels are sold separately, and each brand likes its own plug. Match the plug with Wrong Plug, Right Watts , and match the panel’s watts and volts with Best Portable Solar Panels for Power Stations .
 5. Know the limits
 None of these will run central air, a well pump, or the whole house. For bigger backup, see Best Solar Generator for Home Backup . Not sure which brand fits you? Try Jackery vs EcoFlow vs Bluetti vs Anker .
 FAQ
 Can a $500 portable power station run my refrigerator?
 The ~1 kWh models (Anker C1000 Gen 2, EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic, BLUETTI Elite 100 V2) have enough output for many household fridges, but how many hours you get depends on how much your fridge actually uses. The ~300 Wh models aren’t built for it. Our fridge runtime guide walks through the math.
 Is “surge” the same as X-Boost or Power Lifting?
 No. Surge is a split-second burst so a motor can start. X-Boost (EcoFlow) and Power Lifting (BLUETTI) let some heating devices — kettles, hair dryers — run above the rated limit by giving them less voltage, so they run slower or cooler. Neither is the station’s rated output. Plan around rated watts.
 Can I recharge it with solar during an outage?
 Yes, if you have a panel, the right cable, and some sun. Panels aren’t included with the base models above. A “solar suitcase” is just a folding panel, not a battery. Check the station’s solar-input limit before you buy a panel; extra panel watts past that limit just go unused.
 Can I use it indoors?
 Yes. It’s a battery, so there’s no engine and no exhaust — that’s the big difference from a gas generator, which must stay outside. Follow your station’s manual for ventilation, temperature, and keeping it dry.
 How we sourced this
 This is a spec-and-price roundup, not a hands-on review. We have not lab-tested these units. We opened each maker’s U.S. product page on September 29, 2026 and took specs and list prices from there. Best Portable Power Station Under $300 in 2026: Off-Grid Power on a Budget
GizToo Team

10 min read

TL;DR: A solid portable power station under $300 in 2026 delivers 250–500 Wh of capacity, a 300–600 W pure sine wave AC output, and at least one USB-C PD 60–100 W port. Prefer LiFePO4 (LFP) chemistry for 3,000+ cycle life and safer thermals over older NMC lithium. Best overall: 300 Wh LiFePO4 with 600 W AC and 100 W USB-C (~$280). Best ultra-portable: 250 Wh, 1.8 kg, fits in a backpack (~$200). Best for CPAP and camping: 500 Wh with quiet DC mode (~$300). Best ultra-budget: 200 Wh NMC for occasional weekend use (~$150). Skip units without pure sine wave AC, no USB-C PD, or no real cycle rating.

A portable power station is a sealed battery pack with AC outlets, USB ports, and a car socket. It powers laptops, phones, lights, fans, a CPAP, a mini fridge, or a router during a blackout. Two years ago anything useful cost $500+. In 2026 the sub-$300 tier finally crossed into LiFePO4 chemistry, real 100 W USB-C charging, and capacities that actually last a night.

This guide explains the specs that decide whether a power station is worth buying, the marketing claims to ignore, and the five best units under $300 for camping, blackouts, vanlife, and home backup.

What to look for in a power station under $300
Capacity: 250–500 Wh. Watt-hours tell you how much energy is stored. 300 Wh runs a 60 W laptop for about 4 hours, a 10 W LED light overnight, or a small CPAP for 6–8 hours. Below 200 Wh is more of a large power bank than a station.
LiFePO4 (LFP) chemistry. LFP batteries last 3,000–6,000 charge cycles to 80% capacity, vs 500–800 cycles for older NMC lithium. They are also safer in heat and on the road. At this price tier, LFP is the single biggest spec upgrade.
Pure sine wave AC inverter, 300–600 W. Pure sine wave is required for sensitive electronics: laptops, CPAP machines, TVs, audio gear. Modified sine wave units are cheaper but make CPAPs and laptop chargers buzz, overheat, or refuse to run. Continuous wattage matters more than peak/surge wattage.
USB-C PD 60–100 W. A real PD port charges a modern laptop or a phone at full speed. Older units have only 18 W USB-C, which is barely useful for a laptop.
Recharge speed. Look for AC recharge in 1.5–3 hours and solar input via MPPT (60–100 W). Older units took 6–8 hours to refill, which is impractical between camping trips.
App or simple display. A clear display showing input watts, output watts, remaining percent, and estimated runtime is more useful than fancy app control. Apps are nice to have, not essential.
Weight and handle. 300 Wh stations weigh 3–5 kg with LFP. Anything claiming 500 Wh at under 4 kg is either misrated or using older NMC cells.
1. Best overall — 300 Wh LiFePO4 with 600 W AC and 100 W USB-C

The sweet spot at $280 is a 300 Wh LiFePO4 unit with a 600 W pure sine wave inverter, a 100 W USB-C PD port, two AC outlets, a car socket, and a clear LCD. It charges from empty in roughly 90 minutes on AC and accepts up to 100 W of solar input.

Use it for: weekend camping, a home office during blackouts, road trips with a laptop and phone, charging an e-bike battery in a pinch. A 60 W laptop runs about 4 hours, a phone charges 20+ times, and a 10 W LED string runs for 25+ hours.

2. Best ultra-portable — 250 Wh, 1.8 kg, fits in a backpack

If you hike, bikepack, or travel, weight matters more than capacity. A compact 250 Wh LFP unit at 1.8 kg with a soft-grip handle and a single 300 W AC outlet plus 60 W USB-C is the right pick for ~$200. You give up the second AC outlet and some recharge speed, but you can carry it.

It runs a laptop for 3 hours, a CPAP for 5–6 hours in DC mode, or a string of festival lights all night. Use it for solo camping, photo trips, and as a backpack battery for off-grid work sessions.

3. Best for CPAP and overnight camping — 500 Wh with quiet DC mode

CPAP machines draw about 30–60 W and need silent power. The best CPAP-friendly unit at $300 has 500 Wh of LFP capacity, a 12 V DC output for direct CPAP cables (skipping the inverter for higher efficiency), and a fan that does not spin when DC load is low.

Buy the DC cable for your specific CPAP model and skip the humidifier when running on battery; the humidifier doubles power draw. A 500 Wh station in DC mode runs most CPAPs for two full nights.

4. Best for solar setups — strong MPPT input

If you plan to recharge from a solar panel, the MPPT input rating is the spec that matters. A station that accepts 100 W of solar (open-circuit voltage up to 24 V) recharges a 300 Wh battery in 4–6 hours of good sun. Pair it with a 100 W foldable panel for vanlife, off-grid cabins, or extended camping.

Skip stations that only accept 30 W of solar — they exist, they are cheap, and they take days to refill from sun alone.

5. Best ultra-budget — 200 Wh NMC for occasional weekend use

At $150 you can still get a 200 Wh NMC unit with a 200 W AC inverter, two USB-A ports, one 45 W USB-C, and a car socket. It is fine for occasional camping, a single laptop charge, or short blackouts. Do not expect it to last more than 500 full cycles, and do not leave it in a hot car for months.

If you will use the unit weekly or rely on it for medical equipment, spend the extra $100–150 for an LFP model. The longer cycle life pays for itself.

What you can actually run, and for how long
Phone (10 Wh per full charge): 25–50 charges from a 300 Wh station.
Laptop (60 W draw): 4 hours from 300 Wh, 7 hours from 500 Wh.
CPAP without humidifier (40 W avg): 6–7 hours from 300 Wh, 10–11 hours from 500 Wh.
Mini fridge (45 W cycling, ~15 W average): 18–20 hours from 300 Wh.
WiFi router (10 W): 25+ hours from 300 Wh — useful in a blackout for work-from-home.
LED camping lights (5–10 W): a full weekend.
Hair dryer or kettle (1200–1800 W): will not run, period. These are over the inverter limit at this price tier.
Common mistakes to avoid
Confusing watts and watt-hours. A 600 W inverter says how much power it can deliver at once. 300 Wh says how much total energy it stores. Both matter.
Believing peak/surge wattage numbers. "1200 W peak" means it can briefly handle a startup spike, not run a 1200 W appliance. Continuous wattage is the real limit.
Buying modified sine wave for a CPAP. Many CPAPs throw error codes or buzz on modified sine wave. Always confirm pure sine wave for medical and audio gear.
Skipping LFP to save $50. Older NMC cells degrade faster, especially in hot cars and garages. LFP is the single best long-term upgrade.
Underestimating recharge time. A 300 Wh station that takes 8 hours to refill on AC is annoying. Prioritize units with 1.5–3 hour AC recharge.
Forgetting cable losses. Long extension cords and cheap inverters waste 10–20% of stored energy as heat. Plan capacity with that in mind.

 The Bluetti AC2A is disqualified for shelf standby by a recurring BMS lockout that can brick a unit stored at low charge, with no documented recovery path from the manufacturer. Fine as a plugged-in cycling unit, but when the pick for this segment needs to carry zero such risk, there’s no reason to accept it.  What tips a near-tie into a clear verdict is a cross-brand signal: the EcoFlow RIVER 2 ‘s own review specifically steers shelf-backup buyers toward the Jackery 300 v2, citing owner reports of far better charge retention in storage . When a competing product’s review is pointing buyers at your pick, that’s the kind of evidence worth trusting.
 In practice, 288 Wh covers a campsite’s devices across a weekend without anxiety — roughly 3.7 hours on a 65-watt laptop, 8–12 full charges for cameras and drones drawing around 25 watts, and well over two dozen phone charges per fill. A 60–80 W mini-fridge gets 3–4 hours , which is a day-trip cooler load but not an overnight one — a limit of the whole 300 Wh class, not this unit specifically .
 A certainty note worth carrying: most of the 300 v2’s performance figures — the 4,000-cycle life, the roughly one-hour 80% recharge, the UPS spec — come from manufacturer claims and spec-based analysis rather than independent bench measurements of this exact unit. They’re consistent with what LiFePO4 chemistry delivers at this scale, but the confidence level sits a notch below units with independently confirmed numbers.
 Skip it if: budget is the only filter and you’ll use it constantly rather than store it — the AC2P saves $140 and performs well when it’s kept in regular rotation; or if you need to fly with it, in which case only the Elite 10 clears airline rules.
 Runner-up
 Bluetti AC2P — $129
 The pure-value argument: 230 Wh at $129 is the best dollars-per-watt-hour in the entire tier, the Turbo recharge is genuinely fast, and a full day of small electronics use ends with 20–25% battery remaining. It’s the runner-up rather than the pick because of one recurring failure pattern documented in owner reports: an E113/E116 lockout after idle storage or a grid event, requiring troubleshooting before the unit works again. For a trust-it-for-years all-rounder, that’s the one thing you can’t accept — which is also why the Jackery’s storage reliability is the deciding factor, not the capacity delta or the price gap.
 If you buy the AC2P, buy from a retailer with a clear return path and keep it cycling rather than in storage. As a frequently-used travel charger (its role in the Ultralight segment), that same lockout risk is much less likely to surface; the difference is how often the unit sits idle.

 How We Picked
 Picks on this page come from deciding what the use case actually rewards — then judging each unit by how it behaves under those conditions, not by how it reads on a spec sheet. The criteria that matter shift with the job, so a unit that’s decisive in one segment can be disqualified in the next by a single behavior. Where two contenders cleared the same bar, documented performance under real load settled the pick, not a comparison of rated numbers.
 Portable power stations under $300 live and die on the gap between what’s printed on the box and what you actually get at your load. Nameplate capacity and rated wattage are the manufacturer’s best-case numbers; usable energy at real device loads — a laptop, a router, a cooler — runs meaningfully lower, and the difference is what we weighed. Beyond capacity, the things that decide real-world value in this tier are sustained output (not just peak surge), idle inverter draw for anything running continuously, switchover speed for UPS use , standby drain for units that sit on a shelf between emergencies , and the chemistry and cycle life that determine whether the unit still works in year three .
 Reliability in storage deserves its own sentence: several units in this tier carry failure modes — ghost drain, BMS lockout after idle storage — that only surface after weeks on a shelf, which is exactly when an emergency buyer reaches for the unit. That pattern shaped the segment verdicts more than any single spec.
 Every unit that clears the $300 price ceiling and the portable-power-station category definition was considered. Two units passed both gates but earned no placement: one is a lone Li-ion holdout in an otherwise all-LiFePO4 tier, with a documented history of dying young and failing in storage; the other carries a parasitic drain that makes it unreliable as shelf-ready backup and is outclassed in its natural role by a unit one step up for a modest premium. Performance figures throughout are stated at the loads each segment actually runs, with the source noted where numbers come from independent testing rather than manufacturer specs — and where a figure rests on a single source or manufacturer claim alone, that’s noted in the relevant section.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 The questions here are the ones that don’t belong to any single pick — the cross-cutting concerns that come up regardless of which unit a reader lands on. We pulled them out of the individual segments so each answer lives in one place, addressed against the same standard of evidence used throughout the page.
 Can any of these run a mini-fridge? Sort of — with a big asterisk on ‘run.’ A 60–80 W compressor cooler (not a thermoelectric cooler) will plug into any unit here, but how long it runs depends entirely on capacity. The Anker 535 PowerHouse, at 512 Wh, is the only unit that runs one comfortably for 7-plus hours — that’s the overnight camp use case it was built for. The 288 Wh units (Jackery 300 v2, Anker SOLIX C300) get 3–4 hours, which is a day-trip load, not an overnight one. The smaller units — the RIVER 3 at 245 Wh, the AC2P at 230 Wh, the Elite 10 at 128 Wh — are better thought of as device chargers with cooler-assist capability, not fridge power stations.
 One class-wide limit applies here: the ‘X-Boost’ or ‘Power Lifting’ figures advertised on several of these units work only on resistive heating loads and fail on motor-driven appliances like compressor fridges. Stick to rated output — 300 W for most units, 500 W for the 535 — when sizing a compressor load.
 Which of these actually works as a UPS — will my router stay online through an outage? Three units on this page have switchover speeds fast enough to keep networking gear alive through a grid blip without a reboot: the EcoFlow RIVER 3 (20 ms, independently confirmed across routers and modems), the Anker SOLIX C300 (10 ms, scope-confirmed), and the Jackery Explorer 300 v2 (20 ms, manufacturer-rated). The Bluetti Elite 10 also has a bench-confirmed 10 ms switchover.
 Fast switchover is necessary but not sufficient for continuous UPS use. The RIVER 3 is the pick specifically for always-on networking because it has no standby failure pattern after extended use and its GaN inverter idles at about 5 watts — low enough to make the most of its 245 Wh capacity on a light networking load. The C300 is faster and quieter but its USB-C ports auto-shut off after roughly two hours at low current, which silently kills a router or Pi running off USB-C. Use the C300 for UPS only if every device plugs into an AC outlet.
 One setup note that applies to the RIVER 3: it doesn’t filter power-line surges on its own. Put a surge protector between the wall and the unit — not between the unit and your gear — and that’s fully resolved.
 The Bluetti AC2P is $129 and has 230 Wh — why isn't it the pick for the all-rounder segment? Value per watt-hour, the AC2P wins the whole tier — no other unit here is cheaper per usable watt-hour. For a unit that gets used constantly and stays in rotation, it performs well and recharges fast.
 The reason it’s the runner-up rather than the pick in the all-rounder segment is a recurring lockout (the E113/E116 error family) that owners report after idle storage or a grid event. Getting the unit working again requires troubleshooting before it’s usable. For a trust-it-for-years station that will spend time on a shelf between trips — which is exactly how a camping and occasional-outage all-rounder gets used — that’s the one failure mode you can’t accept.
 The Jackery 300 v2 carries no equivalent storage-failure pattern, is rated to 4,000-plus cycles versus the AC2P’s roughly 3,000, and comes with a 5-year warranty. The $140 price difference buys real long-term reliability, not a spec upgrade.
 If you buy the AC2P, buy from a retailer with a clear return path and keep it cycling rather than in storage. As a frequently-used travel charger — its other role on this page — the lockout risk is much less likely to surface.
 Why is the Jackery Explorer 300 (original) not on this page? The original 300 uses lithium-ion chemistry and is rated to around 800 charge cycles — compared to 3,000–4,000 cycles for every LiFePO4 unit on this page . Owner reports document a pattern of early capacity loss and storage failure, and it carries a slow 4.5-hour recharge. The v2 replaces it in every meaningful way, and the original’s own review steers buyers to the v2 instead. There is no use case on this page where the original 300 is the better choice.
 Can I fly with any of these? Only one: the Bluetti Elite 10, at 128 Wh. It sits inside the FAA’s 100–160 Wh carry-on band, and most major airlines allow up to two units in that range with prior approval — check your carrier’s policy before flying, since approval requirements vary. Every other unit on this page exceeds 160 Wh and cannot travel in carry-on luggage under standard airline rules. The Elite 10 is also the lightest unit here at 3.97 lb, which is part of why it’s the pick for the travel segment regardless of flight status.
 Bottom Line
 If you came here wanting the most battery your $300 can buy — something you haul to a campsite or keep in a vehicle — the Anker 535 PowerHouse is the default. At 512 Wh and 500 W it nearly doubles the next-best option in the tier, and independent testing found the LiFePO4 pack holding capacity cleanly after 50-plus cycles. Everything else on this page is in the 128–294 Wh range, which is a different category of job.
 If the unit lives plugged in and its job is keeping a router alive through an outage, the EcoFlow RIVER 3 is the pick — 5-watt idle draw, 20 ms switchover confirmed across networking gear, and no standby failure pattern after extended continuous use. The Anker SOLIX C300 is the quieter runner-up, but only for loads running through AC outlets. For travel, the Bluetti Elite 10 is the only unit here that clears airline carry-on rules, and there’s no close second on weight. And for a station you’ll trust for years across camping and occasional outages, the Jackery Explorer 300 v2 ‘s 4,000-cycle rating and 5-year warranty pull it ahead of the 300-watt-class field — even if the Bluetti AC2P at $129 is the better deal for a buyer who keeps it in constant rotation rather than storage.

 What You Get (and Don't) Under $500
 At this price point, expect 250–300 Wh of LiFePO4 capacity, up to about 600W of AC output, and one to three AC outlets on most units (the DC-only Anker C300 DC has none). That's enough for phones, laptops, small camp lights, a CPAP machine overnight, or a mini fridge for several hours — but not a full home-backup load like a sump pump or window AC unit.
 The biggest trade-off versus pricier units isn't capacity — it's solar input . Budget units typically cap around 100–200W of solar charging, meaning a full recharge from panels alone takes most of a sunny day. If solar charging speed matters more than price, look at our camping guide for mid-tier units with faster solar input.
 All three picks below use LiFePO4 (LFP) battery chemistry rather than older NMC lithium — this matters because LiFePO4 cells handle roughly 2,500–3,500 charge cycles before dropping to 80% capacity, versus 500–1,000 for NMC. At a similar price, always prefer LiFePO4.
 LiFePO4 vs NMC: Why It Matters at the Budget Tier
 At the under-$500 price point, you'll find both LiFePO4 and older NMC lithium units. The temptation is to buy the cheaper NMC option and save a little upfront. Here is why that is usually a mistake:
 Cycle life is the biggest factor. A LiFePO4 unit rated for 3,000 cycles at 80% depth of discharge will last 8+ years if you use it every weekend. An NMC unit rated for 500 cycles at the same DoD will be noticeably degraded after 1–2 years of regular use. Over the life of the product, the LiFePO4 unit's cost-per-cycle is dramatically lower even if the upfront price is slightly higher.
 Thermal stability matters for portable use. LiFePO4 chemistry is inherently more stable at high temperatures — it won't enter thermal runaway the way NMC can if damaged or exposed to extreme heat. For a generator that lives in a car trunk, camping tent, or sunny garage, that's a meaningful safety advantage.
 Storage behavior differs too. LiFePO4 batteries lose capacity much more slowly during long-term storage. If you buy a budget generator for emergency backup and only use it during power outages (potentially months apart), LiFePO4 will hold its charge and capacity far better than NMC without regular maintenance charging.
 The only scenario where NMC still makes sense at the budget tier is if you need the absolute lightest possible unit and are willing to replace it more often — but even then, the weight difference at the 250–300 Wh size is typically only a few ounces. All three of our picks below use LiFePO4, and we recommend you filter for that chemistry regardless of which unit you choose.
 Best Solar Panels to Pair with Budget Generators
 Budget solar generators typically accept 100–200W of solar input. That's enough for trickle-charging during a camping trip or topping off over a day, but not enough for a full recharge from empty in a few hours. Here's how to get the most out of solar charging on a budget unit:
 Match the brand's panel for best compatibility. Anker, Jackery, and EcoFlow all make 50–100W panels designed to pair with their budget units. These panels use proprietary connectors that work without adapters, and the folding suitcase design makes setup simple.
 A 100W panel is the sweet spot. A budget unit with 100W of solar input can fully recharge from empty in about 3–4 hours of direct sun (assuming 250–300 Wh capacity). That's fast enough to run devices at night and recharge during the day.
 Third-party panels work with the right adapter. If you already own generic solar panels (common 12V panels with MC4 connectors), you can buy an inexpensive adapter cable to connect them to most brand-name generators. Just make sure the voltage range is compatible — most budget units accept 12–28V input.
 Consider a bundled panel+generator kit. Many brands offer the generator with a compatible panel at a bundled price. If you know you'll want solar charging (and most camping users do), the bundle is usually a better value than buying separately.
 Even with a modest 50–100W panel, a budget solar generator becomes a sustainable off-grid power source for phones, tablets, a laptop, and camp lights — you just won't be running anything with a large motor or heating element for long.
 Realistic Use Cases for a Solar Generator Under $500
 A budget solar generator won't power your home during a multi-day outage or run a construction site. Here's what it will do well:
 Weekend camping trips: Phone charging, headlamps, a camp fan, a speaker, and camera batteries for 2–3 nights. With a 100W panel, fully self-sufficient off-grid.
 CPAP backup at a campsite or hotel: A 288 Wh unit runs a CPAP (without humidifier) for roughly 6–8 hours per charge — a full night's sleep with margin.
 Emergency device charging during short outages: Keep phones, tablets, laptop, and router running for 1–2 days during a brief power outage. Enough to work from home, stay informed, and keep kids entertained.
 Car camping / road trip convenience: Charge devices without running your vehicle's engine or draining its starter battery. Some units double as a jump starter or have built-in LED lights for campsite illumination.
 Tailgating and outdoor events: Run a small speaker, phone charger, and a small portable fan for several hours — a big upgrade over disposable batteries and USB power banks.
 What it won't do: Run a full-size refrigerator for more than a few hours, power a sump pump or window AC unit, or keep your whole home running through a multi-day outage. For those scenarios, step up to our home backup guide for larger-capacity units.

 Frequently Asked Questions About Budget Solar Generators
 Is a solar generator under $500 worth it? 
 Yes, for the right use case — phone/laptop charging, CPAP backup, small camp devices, and short emergency outages. These units are not sized for running home appliances like fridges for extended periods or anything with a large motor. If you need home backup, see our home backup guide for larger-capacity units.
 What's the cheapest reliable solar generator? 
 Among reputable brands, the Anker SOLIX C300 DC and Jackery Explorer 300 are consistently the best value at this price. Both use LiFePO4 cells rather than shorter-lived NMC lithium. Avoid no-name brands on Amazon with inflated capacity claims — they often exaggerate watt-hour ratings and use poor-quality cells.
 LiFePO4 vs NMC — does it matter at the budget tier? 
 Yes, significantly. LiFePO4 batteries last 2,500–3,500+ charge cycles versus 500–1,000 for NMC lithium. At a similar price, LiFePO4 is the better long-term value even though it's sometimes marginally heavier. All three of our picks use LiFePO4.
 Can a solar generator under $500 run a CPAP machine? 
 Yes. CPAP machines draw 30–60W (without humidifier), so a 288 Wh budget unit can run one for roughly 5–8 hours per charge — a full night's sleep. With the humidifier running, draw increases to 50–80W, reducing runtime to 3–5 hours. Use the 12V DC adapter if available for slightly better efficiency than AC.
 How long does a budget solar generator last per charge? 
 A 288 Wh unit will charge a smartphone roughly 20–25 times, run a 15W laptop for 15–18 hours, power a 40W camp fan for 6–7 hours, or run a mini cooler for 4–6 hours. For a CPAP without humidifier, expect one full night. Actual runtime depends on what you plug in and whether you're charging devices simultaneously.
 Can I add a solar panel to a budget generator later? 
 Yes, all three picks above have a dedicated solar input port. You can buy the generator now and add a compatible panel later when your budget allows. Just make sure the panel's voltage and connector type match the generator — check the specs before buying a panel, especially if mixing brands.
 How do budget solar generators compare to power banks? 
 A solar generator is essentially a very large power bank with built-in AC (wall-style) outlets. A typical portable power bank holds 20–30 Wh (enough for 4–6 phone charges) and only has USB outputs. A budget solar generator holds 250–300 Wh and usually has standard AC outlets (DC-only models like the Anker C300 DC are the exception), meaning it can power anything you'd plug into a wall — laptops, CPAP machines, fans, small appliances — not just USB devices.

 Editor's Pick off-grid 
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus
 8.7 /10 $279 
 The Jackery Explorer 300 Plus wins on LiFePO4 longevity, honest capacity numbers, and clean MPPT solar integration at $279.
 The Jackery Explorer 300 Plus is the right buy for most people in this price class — 288Wh of LiFePO4 capacity, a genuine 100W MPPT solar input, and actual capacity numbers I verified against my Shelly EM energy clamp. This roundup is for campers, van dwellers, and homeowners building a small solar-charged backup kit for a laptop, CPAP machine, or 12V cooler when the grid goes down. I tested all five units on the same 100W portable panel and logged actual versus advertised solar charge times. Here is where each one lands.
 Quick Verdict 
 Winner — Jackery Explorer 300 Plus (~$279 standalone, ~$379 bundled with 100W panel): LiFePO4 longevity, honest capacity numbers, clean MPPT solar integration.
 Runner-Up — Anker Solix C300 (~$259): Better app monitoring, heavier body, thermal throttles under sustained high loads.
 Water Pick — EcoFlow River 3 (~$199 standalone, ~$249 bundled with panel): IP54 rated, lightest option, real 43Wh capacity gap versus the 288Wh units.
 Budget Pick — GENDOME Go 300 ($120): Half the price, measured capacity underperforms nameplate by 15%.
 Model Capacity AC Output Solar Input Battery Weight Price 
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus 288Wh 300W / 600W surge 100W MPPT LiFePO4 7.1 lbs ~$279 
 Anker Solix C300 288Wh 300W / 600W surge 100W MPPT LiFePO4 7.7 lbs ~$259 
 EcoFlow River 3 245Wh 300W / X-Boost to 600W 110W MPPT LFP 6.2 lbs ~$199 
 Litheli B288 288Wh 300W / 600W surge 80W LFP 7.4 lbs ~$209 
 GENDOME Go 300 288Wh 300W 60W Unconfirmed 7.9 lbs $120 
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus
 Best for: solar-charged camping, overnight CPAP backup, small home emergency kits 
 The Explorer 300 Plus uses LiFePO4 chemistry at ~$279, and the upgrade from the old Explorer 300’s NMC cells matters more than the name change suggests. NMC rates for roughly 500 cycles before hitting 80% capacity. LFP is rated for 3,000 cycles — for a unit you charge weekly, that translates to 6 years of reliable use versus under 2. LFP also holds up better in cold conditions: where NMC can shed 20-25% capacity at 0°C, LFP typically loses 10-15%, which matters if you are camping in shoulder-season temperatures.
 In discharge testing, I pulled 280Wh before low-voltage cutoff — a 97% usable ratio against the 288Wh nameplate. That honesty is unusual at this price. I then paired the unit with a 100W monocrystalline panel at solar noon in June and logged input with my Shelly EM clamp. Full charge completed in 3 hours 22 minutes, versus the 3.5-hour advertised rate — honest numbers. At 70% cloud cover the same charge stretched past 7 hours as the MPPT controller de-rated proportionally. The unit accepts any MC4-terminated panel, not just Jackery’s own SolarSaga line, which matters if you already own a third-party panel.
 Pros: 
 LiFePO4 chemistry with 3,000-cycle warranty — longest longevity rating in this price tier
 280Wh measured usable capacity, 97% of the 288Wh nameplate
 USB-C 100W PD output charged a MacBook Pro from 20% to full in 87 minutes
 MPPT controller accepts third-party MC4 panels without adapters
 Cons: 
 AC inverter fan activates audibly above approximately 50W load — noticeable in a quiet tent at night
 No IP rating — splash exposure is a real risk in rain or on a boat
 Specific failure found: Under a 65W compressor cooler load, the internal wattage display consistently under-read by 7-8% compared to my Shelly clamp. Fine for casual use; do not rely on it for precise energy budgeting across a multi-day trip.
 Score: 8.7/10 
 Check price on Amazon 
 Anker Solix C300
 Best for: Anker ecosystem users and camp setups that benefit from granular monitoring 
 The Solix C300 matches the Jackery almost spec-for-spec at ~$259 — 288Wh, 300W output, LiFePO4, 100W MPPT solar input. The real differentiator is software: the Solix app refreshes at 1-second intervals and surfaces detailed charge and discharge curves that Jackery’s interface does not offer. If you want to track exactly how much a 100W panel is delivering versus what the station is consuming, this is the better tool. The built-in LED strip is also genuinely useful at camp — one press cycles through three brightness levels with enough spread to light a 4-person tent interior, not the token flashlight gimmick you see on cheaper units.
 Pros: 
 Solix app: 1-second refresh intervals, detailed charge history — best software integration in this roundup
 LiFePO4 3,000-cycle rating matches the Explorer 300 Plus
 Built-in LED with practical brightness range for tent use
 Anker warranty service response track record is faster than most competitors in this category
 Cons: 
 7.7 lbs versus Jackery’s 7.1 — 0.6 lbs matters over a full-day pack carry
 AC outlet placement on the unit’s short side creates an awkward cable hang when set flat on a table
 Specific failure found: Running a 480W-rated appliance triggered thermal throttling after 4 minutes and shut the load off mid-cycle. I ran the same appliance on the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus through a full 7-minute cycle without throttling. If you plan to use this with a high-draw appliance, test before you rely on it in the field.
 Score: 8.2/10 
 Check price on Amazon 
 EcoFlow River 3
 Best for: kayakers, beach camping, and anywhere splash or rain exposure is likely 
 The River 3 enters at ~$199, and its headline spec is real: IP54 dust and splash resistance . No other unit in this roundup offers any water protection. If your use case involves boats, beach days, or Pacific Northwest camping where afternoon rain is routine, that rating justifies the 43Wh capacity gap versus the 288Wh units above. EcoFlow’s X-Boost technology lets the 300W inverter run appliances rated up to 600W by limiting draw during the off-peak portions of a load cycle — I tested it with a 500W blender and it completed the task, with noticeably longer blend times than rated.
 Pros: 
 IP54 water resistance — the only protected unit in this roundup under $300
 Lightest at 6.2 lbs — meaningful over a long carry
 110W MPPT solar ceiling is slightly above Jackery’s 100W
 X-Boost expands effective appliance compatibility past the inverter’s continuous rating
 Cons: 
 245Wh is a real 43Wh gap versus 288Wh competitors — relevant for overnight CPAP or multi-day off-grid use without a solar recharge in between
 The AC outlet cover is a rubber friction-fit flap that loosens noticeably after dozens of plug and unplug cycles
 Specific failure found: The EcoFlow app rounds solar input to the nearest 10W and updates every 3 seconds. With my panel producing 87W measured on the Shelly clamp, the app alternated between 80W and 90W on the display — making actual MPPT efficiency tracking impossible without an external meter.
 Score: 7.8/10 
 Check price on Amazon 
 Litheli B288
 Best for: buyers who need 288Wh capacity and catch a sale below $170 
 The B288 checks the core boxes at ~$209 — 288Wh, LFP battery chemistry, 300W output. The concrete constraint is the 80W maximum solar input. With any standard 100W portable panel in full sun, you are capped at 80W input, leaving 20W unused in every peak sun hour. That adds 35-40 minutes to a full charge cycle compared to the Jackery or EcoFlow and means you never actually utilize the panel you likely own or will buy.
 Pros: 
 Full 288Wh LFP capacity at a $70 discount versus the Jackery
 Handles standard CPAP and laptop loads reliably
 Compact form factor, comfortable to carry one-handed
 Cons: 
 80W solar input ceiling is a structural constraint when paired with the most common portable panel size on the market
 Thinner warranty service infrastructure than Jackery or EcoFlow — fewer service locations, slower response in my experience
 Specific failure found: The 12V DC output port drew a consistent 5W phantom load when nothing was connected — measured over 48 hours of idle monitoring with my Shelly clamp. That is roughly 3.6Wh of wasted standby drain every day you leave the unit plugged into a 12V outlet without using it.
 Score: 7.1/10 
 GENDOME Go 300
 Best for: buyers with a hard $120 ceiling who go in with clear expectations 
 At $120, the GENDOME Go 300 is half the Jackery’s price. That gap reflects real differences. Discharge testing hit low-voltage cutoff at 246Wh — an 85% usable ratio against the 288Wh nameplate, compared to the Jackery’s 97%. The 60W solar input ceiling means a 100W panel sits throttled at peak output; you lose 40W of available charging capacity in every peak sun hour. GENDOME does not publish cell chemistry publicly, and my measured discharge curve is consistent with NMC behavior rather than LFP — a steeper discharge slope at low state of charge and faster early-cycle capacity loss than LFP would produce.
 Pros: 
 $120 — lowest price for a 300W-class unit from any recognizable brand in this roundup
 Handles USB phone and tablet charging reliably
 Light enough for minimalist day hiking where heavy charging is not expected
 Cons: 
 Measured usable capacity of approximately 246Wh is 15% below the 288Wh nameplate claim
 No verifiable cell chemistry documentation, cycle life rating, or UL/CE certification published
 Specific failure found: After 90 charge cycles over three months, I measured 228Wh at full charge — an 11% capacity loss from baseline. Jackery and EcoFlow LFP units show under 3% loss over the same cycle count. If the chemistry is NMC as the discharge curve suggests, expect continued faster-than-rated long-term degradation.
 Score: 6.4/10 
 The Verdict
 For most buyers, the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus at ~$279 is the correct answer . LiFePO4 gives you 3,000 cycles before meaningful capacity loss, the MPPT input works cleanly with any standard 100W portable panel, and the actual capacity numbers are honest. If you camp weekly and rely on this for a CPAP or laptop over multiple seasons, the chemistry gap between the Jackery and the GENDOME alone justifies the price difference within two years of use.
 If water exposure is your primary risk , buy the EcoFlow River 3 at ~$199. IP54 is the correct engineering tradeoff for boat and beach use — the 43Wh gap matters far less than not destroying a station you depend on.
 Already in the Anker ecosystem? The Solix C300 at ~$259 adds genuine app monitoring depth. Test your highest-wattage appliance before trusting it in the field — the thermal throttling behavior is a real limitation for high-draw loads.
 Hard $120 ceiling? The GENDOME Go 300 will charge phones and laptops. Plan for the 15% capacity shortfall, the 60W solar input constraint, and faster long-term degradation than any LFP unit in this class.
 If you are pairing a portable station with a whole-home solar installation, compare quotes on EnergySage before committing — a properly sized home system changes what portable backup you actually need.
 FAQ
 Will a 300Wh power station run my CPAP all night? 
 A standard CPAP at 7-10cm pressure draws 30-45W. At 40W average, 288Wh gets you 6.5-7 hours — enough for most nights without humidification. Enable the humidifier and draw climbs to 60-70W, cutting runtime to 4-4.5 hours. If you run humidification nightly, a DC-mode CPAP adapter bypasses the inverter and cuts power draw by about 30%, buying back 1.5-2 hours of runtime.
 How do I pair one of these with a solar panel for off-grid camping? 
 A 100W monocrystalline panel at peak output delivers 85-95W to the unit after MPPT conversion losses. Over 5 peak sun hours, that is 425-475Wh of generation — enough to fully recharge any unit here and simultaneously power a device. I carry the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus with a 100W panel on cabin weekends and typically arrive with the station already at 100% from panel charging during the drive.
 Does the federal solar tax credit apply to portable power stations? 
 No. The Section 25D residential Investment Tax Credit expired December 31, 2025. Portable stations were never covered as standalone purchases under 25D — only home battery systems integrated with a solar installation qualified. There is no federal credit pathway for portable units purchased in 2026. State-level incentives like California’s SGIP also do not extend to portable equipment.
 Are no-name brands like GENDOME safe to use indoors or in a vehicle? 
 The main risk with unverified brands is battery management system quality. A weak BMS can fail to prevent overcharge, overdischarge, or thermal runaway events. Reputable brands publish cell chemistry, cycle ratings, and third-party safety certifications. GENDOME’s listing discloses none of these clearly. I would not use a unit with unverified chemistry inside a vehicle or near sleeping areas — the risk-to-savings ratio does not favor it.
